title: The head's phrasebook
allegory: An OV circuit is like a head's phrasebook: once the head has decided which word to look at, it opens the phrasebook to that word's page and reads out which next words to vote for, and a copying head's phrasebook simply says each word back.
map: the phrasebook, one page per word the head might look at
the full OV circuit W_E W_V W_O W_U: a d_vocab × d_vocab matrix
opening to the page of the word you looked at
a row: that source token's embedding pushed through W_V W_O
reading the page out as votes for next words
a phrasebook that says each word back to itself
a copying head: the diagonal dominates
two clerks who always look at the same page
heads with the same attention pattern: only their summed OV circuit is the real one
credit: The 'where to look versus what to write' split is from Elhage et al., A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (Anthropic, 2021).

chapters.name: Four opaque grids
chapters.note: W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O... which one says what it does?

cap.1: An attention head has four grids of numbers. Stare at any one alone and it tells you nothing about what the head actually does.
cap.2: W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O are not separately meaningful. They only ever act in pairs, and each pair answers one clear question.
cap.3: The four matrices only enter as two low-rank products: W_QK sets attention scores and W_OV sets what is written (Elhage et al., 2021). The individual factors are not separately meaningful.

cap.1: Split the job in two. One pair of grids picks which earlier word to look at. The other pair is a phrasebook: it says what to write about that word.
cap.2: QK decides where a head looks; OV decides what it writes once it looks there. OV never asks why the head looked; it just maps the looked-at token to an output.
cap.3: Given the attention pattern, the head's output is linear in the source residual via W_OV. Along the direct path, the OV circuit is a fixed map from attended token to logit effect.

cap.1: Four steps: turn the looked-at word into a vector, read it, write it, turn the result into votes for next words. Multiply them: that is the phrasebook.
cap.2: W_E W_V W_O W_U is a d_vocab × d_vocab table: row = token attended to, column = logit it pushes. It is low rank through d_head = 64, so keep it as a FactoredMatrix.
cap.3: Full OV circuit W_E W_OV W_U has rank at most d_head. FactoredMatrix keeps the factors, giving svd, norms and top-k without materialising a d_vocab² matrix you cannot fit in memory.

cap.1: For a head that copies, the phrasebook's rule is simple: whatever word you looked at, say that word. The big entries run down the diagonal.
cap.2: A copying head has an OV circuit whose diagonal dominates. The exercise scores it with top_1_acc: the fraction of rows whose biggest entry sits on the diagonal.
cap.3: Copying means diagonal dominance of W_E W_OV W_U. top_1_acc measures argmax-on-diagonal per row; induction heads and IOI's name movers are the copiers you will test.

cap.1: Head 1.4 puts its biggest vote on the diagonal in only 31% of rows, as if it barely copies. Add its twin, head 1.10, and the score jumps to about 96%.
cap.2: 1.4 alone: top-1 30.79%, top-5 47.73%. Heads 1.4 and 1.10 share an attention pattern, so the stream gets their summed writes. Score the sum: 95.6% top-1, 98% top-5.
cap.3: The effective circuit is W_E (W_OV of 1.4 + W_OV of 1.10) W_U: same attention, so contributions add before W_U. Individually mediocre, jointly excellent; nothing pushes either to copy alone.

chapters.name: Weights versus runs

left.title: OV circuit (weights)
lines: what the head would write for any token

right.title: Logit attribution (a run)
lines: what it actually wrote this time

chapters.verdict: The phrasebook says what a head can say; a run shows what it did say.

cap.1: Reading the phrasebook needs no example sentences at all: it tells you what the head would say about any word. A real sentence shows what it did say.
cap.2: The OV circuit is weights-only: no data, no forward pass. Direct logit attribution is its activation-based cousin: on one prompt, what did this head actually push?
cap.3: Weights-only analysis is a claim about a path, so check it is the whole path the stream receives. Activation methods such as DLA and patching answer the prompt-specific question.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: QK: where to look. OV: what to write.

cap.1: Splitting a head into 'where it looks' and 'what it says' lets you read circuits off the weights. Copying returns in induction and name-mover heads.
cap.2: IOI's name-mover heads copy a name into the logits, so their OV circuits are copiers too. Always check for twin heads before trusting a single-head score.
cap.3: Reading OV circuits turns weights into checkable claims like 'this head copies': a foundation for understanding a model and, eventually, for editing or steering it precisely.

coda.title: A head's phrasebook: rows are words it looked at, columns are words it votes for

readouts.label: this head's copying score (top-1 on the diagonal)
readouts.f: round(100 * G.filter((row, r) => row.every((v, c) => c == r || v < row[r])).length / G.length) + '%'

readouts.label: with its twin head's writes added
readouts.f: (T => round(100 * G.map((row, r) => row.map((v, c) => v + T(r, c))).filter((row, r) => row.every((v, c) => c == r || v < row[r])).length / G.length) + '%')((r, c) => r % 2 == 1 && r == c ? 3 : (r % 2 == 0 && c == (r + 2) % 6 ? 1 : 0))

caption.1: Each row is a word the head looked at; tap cells to add votes. The score counts rows whose biggest vote is the same word. That is copying.
caption.2: This head copies on half the rows and votes for a neighbour on the rest: 50%. Its twin looks at the same places, so add their tables and the diagonal wins nearly everywhere.
caption.3: top_1_acc over rows of W_E W_OV W_U. With shared attention the stream receives the sum of both heads' W_OV, so score the sum: ARENA's 1.4 goes from 30.79% alone to 95.6% with 1.10.

where_else: Name-mover heads in IOI: OV circuits that copy a name into the logits
Induction heads: the copying half of the circuit that continues repeated text
The direct path W_E W_U, read the same way as a table of which token tends to follow which

hamming.what: A head's value and output weights, sandwiched between embedding and unembedding and read as a table from 'token attended to' to 'logits pushed'.
hamming.when: Whenever you want to know what a head writes regardless of any particular prompt, for example to test whether it copies.
hamming.why: It turns four opaque matrices into one readable map, so claims like 'this head copies' can be checked straight from the weights.

object.title: The phrasebook landscape
object.subtitle: Two heads' phrasebooks as a field of bars: rows are words looked at, columns are words voted for.

cap.1: One head's phrasebook as a landscape: rows are words it looked at, columns are words it votes for. Only half the rows peak on the diagonal.
cap.2: Head A alone copies on every other row and votes for the next word on the rest. Copying score: 50%.
cap.3: A single head's full OV circuit with diagonal dominance on half the rows, so top_1_acc = 0.5.

cap.1: Its twin looks at exactly the same places and fills in the other half.
cap.2: Head B alone copies precisely where A does not. On its own it also scores 50%.
cap.3: Heads that share an attention pattern are free to split the work; neither needs to copy well alone.

cap.1: Add the two phrasebooks and a clean ridge runs down the diagonal: together they copy.
cap.2: The stream receives both heads' writes, so the real circuit is the sum: 100% on this toy, 95.6% for ARENA's heads 1.4 + 1.10.
cap.3: Effective OV = W_E (W_OV^A + W_OV^B) W_U. Score the summed path: in ARENA, 30.79% alone becomes 95.6% summed.

cap.1: From above, the diagonal is the signature of copying: look at a word, say that word.
cap.2: Diagonal dominance is what you expect from induction heads and IOI's name movers.
cap.3: A copying head approximates the identity on token space through a map of rank at most d_head.

predict.q: A head's OV circuit scores 31% on the copying test. What should you check before deciding it does not copy?

options.t: Whether another head shares its attention pattern
Whether the model trained for long enough

predict.why: Heads that look at the same places add their writes. Score the summed circuit: for 1.4 plus 1.10 that took 30.79% to 95.6%.

predict.q: The full OV circuit is a vocabulary-by-vocabulary table, about 50k by 50k. How do you work with it?

options.t: Keep it factored and compute from the factors
Build the full table on the GPU

predict.why: It has rank at most d_head = 64, so the factors hold everything. FactoredMatrix gives svd, norms and top-k without the dense table, which would not fit in memory.

object.where: Any lookup table read straight off a model's weights: the direct path's bigram table, embedding similarity maps.
